Our wheat was available for export earlier than was usual, and our railways were able to comfortably take care of that export, but financial conditions actually compelled heavy sales of our export wheat in those months of last year, with the result that Canadian wheat declined relatively more than any other wheat of the world which went upon the British market. And while this of course explains a great deal of the abnormal rise in values of our exports of last year, it does not necessarily follow that it was a profitable export trade.
I might say the same thing in connection with the export of oats. I have not the figures, but I understand that our western provinces exported to the United States- that export being made possible by the reduction of duty on oats to six cents a bushel in the United States tariff-24,000,000 bushels of oats which would not ordinarily have gone to the United States, this being a further explanation of the abnormal exports of last year. These figures indicate that the export figures of the present fiscal year will not, upon reflection, appear so favourable by reason of the fact that a great deal of our exports which usually would be credited to the present fiscal year are credited to last year, thus accounting for the abnormal increase in our figures.
This is the appropriate occasion for a discussion of the expenditures of the Government. I ask the attention of the House while I discuss this matter generally and with some degree of detail. A very prominent economist has said: ' The question of expenditure is just as much a financial problem as that of revehue,
4 p.m. neither in theory nor in practice is it advisable to separate them so completely.' Mr. Gladstone once very justly remarked: 'Good finance consists more in the spending than in the collection of revenue.' I submit that these two views should be accepted as axiomatic in *the matter of public expenditure. Particularly is this true of a large country, rich in undeveloped natural resources, and where a system' of popular government prevails. It is fast becoming evident to all reflecting citizens of qur country that we are extravagant in the disposition of our national wealth and income for purposes that frequently are both unnecessary and unproductive, and devoid of sound business principles. I am not ascribing all the blame to bon. gentlemen opposite. BotA poli-

tical parties must assume responsibility in this respect. It is time, however, for a * fundamental change in the character of public expenditure. All public expenditure should answer some substantial purposes or it should not be tolerated.
When out of power the Government party were emphatic and insistent that the late Government were grossly extravagant in expenditure. In the opinion of hon. gentlemen opposite the annual expenditure was so large as to constitute, in the judgment of the Prime Minister, prima facie evidence of corrupt expenditure. It was said that controllable expenditure was so excessive as to be criminally wasteful. To-day it is very much higher, yet we hear no apology or admission of extravagance, criminal or otherwise. They promised much in the way of establishing sounder principles for public expenditure, but so far, their record for reckless expenditure, and expenditure without principle, is without a parallel in our financial history. Their high sounding promises in respect to public expenditure is but as a tale that is told. Never for a moment since their entrance to office, have they disclosed or professed a desire for sound business expenditure.
' Dash away and spend the money ' was the openly expressed injunction of an hon. gentleman opposite this session to the Government. There was no need on the part of the member from Prince Edward Island to inculcate this principle for the guidance of the present Government. They have given ample evidence of their gifts in this direction, although it required the frankness of a private member supporting the Ministry to acknowledge publicly what we all believed to be true, namely, that the Government are more interested and ' concerned in devising means for the expenditure of the revenue than for providing the requisite revenue for necessary and legitimate expenditure. I remarked last year that it ordinarily was the function of Government first to fix its budget of expenditures, and then provide the revenue by taxation, but it is obviously the practice of the Government to obtain all the revenue possible, and then provide means of expending it. As I said last year, the Committee of Supply has become merely the committee of ways and means to spend the revenue. Yes, ' dash away and spend the money ' is the open and avowed programme of the Government. I trust this policy will not receive the support of the people of Canada who are providing the money.

But the Government reply: The Opposition party do not object to the items of Supply voted from time to time. This is a weak and fatuous defence. No opposition has the opportunity of discussing in detail the items of the Expropriation Bill. Protest availeth nothing when it is possible even. The Government must take the full responsibility of its own supply and expenditure. They alone are responsible, and I charge that they are needlessly prodigal in this respect, and are not in any degree, it would appear, guided by principle or policy. Witness the utter lack of principle in the increase of subsidies to one province in the first session of Parliament. What more reprehensible than the arbitration reference provided for aiding British Columbia in its mad policy of expenditure, as if there was anything to arbitrate? Conceding that the province was justly entitled to an increase of provincial subsidies, I say nevertheless that the submission of such a matter to arbitration, when there was no issue to arbitrate, was a piece of administrative folly that should wreck immediately the strongest Administration that ever held office. That one act alone should be regarded by reflecting people as a sufficient ground for a vote of want of confidence in the Government at the first opportunity.
Take the expenses incurred to-day in connection with Fenian Raid bounties. Speaking for myself, I say that the administration of that Act is nothing more or less to-day than a public scandal, and I say that although the people of my province will probably benefit more by the bounties than the people of any other province. Not the slightest business-like attention is given to the administration of the Fenian Raid Bounties Act. In fact, in a by-election in the province of Nova Scotia recently promises were made by prominent supporters of this Government that improper applications for the bounty would be condoned through the influence of prominent Conservatives in that county with the Government administration. It is quite proper to give the Fenian Raid bounty to those who are entitled to it. But I want to tell the Minister of Finance that it would be worth his while to. see that the Fenian Raid bounties are paid promptly and in business-like way and it would certainly be worth his while to inquire how much of the public money of this country is being improperly expended in that connection. To illustrate
the peculiar methods adopted tjy hon. gentlemen opposite in making expenditures, let me refer to another matter. We are promised legislation this year to provide moneys wherewith to reimburse the depositors of the Farmers' Bank. If that legislation is introduced, if the money is voted and subsequently paid to the losing depositors of that defunct banking institution, it will not be because of any sympathy on the part of the Government with those who lost their money in the failure of that bank, it will not be because of any principle, but it will be because this Government want to pay the election expenses of their own friends in the last Dominion election. That is a pretty strong statement and perhaps requiring some little explanation, but I have no doubt hon. gentlemen opposite can understand my meaning very well indeed. Many hon. gentlemen now occupying seats on the other side of the House, in the election of 1911, promised that if their party was returned to power, the depositors, at least, of the Farmers' Bank would be refunded their losses by the Government of this country. That was a corrupt bargain to make as between a candidate and the electorate to which he was appealing. If he were using his own money it would be a corrupt bargain; but there would not perhaps be so much objection to it, as to those hon. gentlemen who have secured seats in Parliament coming to the Government and saying:	I cannot liquidate the promises I
made to the depositors of the Farmers' Bank, myself, as I have not the money, will the Minister of Finance he good enough to do it for me. I repeat that if that expenditure is made it will be absolutely devoid of principle as are many of the other expenditures made by the present Administration.	_
Now let us investigate briefly the actual expenditures of the present Government. In the year ending March 31, 1912,-and the Government was not responsible for the Appropriation Act of that year,-the expenditure chargeable against revenue, amounted to $98,161,440.77, in 1913 it had grown to $112,059,537.41; for 1914 the estimate is $129,000,000, and for 1914-15 it doubtless will reach $150,000,000. The Expropriation Act for this year will provide for expenditures on consolidated fund account in excess of $146,000,000, and the Supplementaries will contain a substantial amount also. detectaphone had been within range of tha hon. gentleman in that election, and that it were here to-day, so that we could hear its record. I will accept the hon. gentleman's statement that he never used the exact words which I have suggested; but if he will give to me and to the House the exact words he used in discussing privately and publicly the tax upon agricultural

implements, I will merely ask that he allow me to interpret the meaning.
I know that my hon. friend the Solicitor General (Mr. Meighen) would not place himself in such a compromising position as to display the banner: 'Vote for Meighen and free agricultural implements.' He is a very skilful dialectician, and he knows how to make a statement that is open to many constructions. I know that my hon. friend never promised free agricultural implements in the last campaign, but he will not deny that many people in his constituency thought he did promise it.
I have never met one.

I see my hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Davidson) in the Chamber. He was in favour of free agricultural implements, and yet he voted against it the other night. I have in my possession a card which he circulated amongst his very intelligent electors, and it was a strange one. His slogan was: 'One King, one flag, one fleet-and free agricultural implements.' This is rather an anticlimax to a trinity of election platitudes which did not mean much and which my hon. friend did not intend to mean much, but he gave the cry of free agricultural implements a royal and imperial importance by ranking his policy for free agricultural implements with: one King, one flag and one fleet.
The Minister of Finance advised us yesterday that he had had the advantage of special information respecting agricultural implements. He said:
We have made inquiries. For considerably over a year past we have been making inquiries and investigations into the question of agricultural implements. We have made an investigation into the prices of agricultural implements on both sides of the line, in Canada and in the United States. We have made an inquiry as to the factory cost of production of the principal agricultural implements in Canada and in the United States. We have examined the balance sheets of manufacturers with the idea of ascertaining what their position is and whether or not they are making undue profit upon their business.
I think it is only fair that when the House goes into Committee of Ways and Means we should have the advantage of the researches of the Department of Finance into the agricultural implement industry and that we should have all the knowledge which the hon. minister has respecting the balance sheets of the respective manufacturers of implements on this continent. I trust it is the intention of the minister to

give us this information. When we have that 1 am sure that we on this side of the House will be pleased to engage in a fair and businesslike discussion of the tariff upon agricultural implements-and there I must leave the subject.
I wish to discuss at some little length the question of removal of duty upon wheat in chis country in order to secure from the United States admission into that country of our wheat and flour. I also wish to discuss the policy enunciated by my distinguished leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) in favour of the principle of the elimination of the duty upon staple foodstuffs in order to secure for the people of this country the vital necessaries of life, food-
5 p.m. stuffs, at the lowest possible price, which is a pressing, serious human problem for us who are the representatives of the people to discuss and legislate upon in this Parliament. Dealing first with the question of wheat, the United States Government in effect say to the Government of this country: If you place wheat upon the free list you can have entry into our market for wheat and wheat products, inclusive of wheat flour. Members upon this side of the House say it should be done. We proposed a resolution to that effect only a few weeks ago. Hon. gentlemen opposite say it should not be done and that Canada should maintain the duty as it now stands. The issue is clear, clean-cut and well defined. It is an interesting issue to debate It is one of great interest and importance to this country. I believe that the position that we upon this side take upon this question is the correct one. I believe that the position which the hon. gentlemen opposite take, is wrong and cannot be supported, and I do not think that they have up to this moment given-us, or that they will be able in the future to give us, reasons which will sustain and justify the position which they assume . in respect to this question. There are many people in this country who will sustain the Liberal party in the position which they take respecting the wheat duty. I think that the people of the Prairie provinces almost unanimously will do so. The Legislature of the province of Manitoba passed a resolution on this subject and, as hon. gentlemen know, the dominant party in that Legislature is one in sympathy with hon. gentlemen opposite. In fact, it is this "" Legislature which gave this Government its present Minister of Public Works, and I have no doubt that that hon. gentleman is

still strong and influential in the councils ol the government party in the province of Manitoba. That resolution reads:
Whereas the Congress of the United States of America have by recent legislation reduced the duty on wheat and wheat products entering the said United States of America.
And whereas provision has been made in the said legislation for the total removal of such duty on wheat entering the United States of America from any foreign country who would likewise remove such duty.
And whereas it is the opinion of this House that the removal of such duty by the Govern-nv t of the Dominion of Canada from the United States of America would be beneficial to the agriculturalists of Manitoba.
Therefore let it he resolved that in the opinion of this House the Parliament of Canada should enact such legislation as would give the farmers of Manitoba the benefit of the countervailing duty on wheat and wheat products as provided in the Underwood tariff.
T!i is is an important question. I do not wish to say, even though I may think so, that there is nothing in the contention of hon. gentlemen opposite.
Let us take the wheat industry in our northwest and ascertain, if we can, the present condition of that industry, and what its future prospects, so far as we may safely venture. And I refer to the prairie provinces, because it is the seat of the major portion of our wheat production. Let me first call attention to the relative importance of this industry in Canada.
The total value of our exports of agricultural produce to all countries in 1913 was $150,000,000 cf which wheat and wheat flour comprised over $107,000,000. Wheat and its flour comprised in 1913 in value nearly 75 per cent of our exports of agricultural produce to the United Kingdom, and over 30 per cent of our total exports of Canadian productions of all kinds. Those figures alone will sufficiently impress one with the importance of the wheat industry alone; while there is much to say about other natural productions in that part of Canada.
Now, what are some of the outstanding facts regarding the actual condition of the industry at the present moment, and what I am about to say is applicable to the grain industry as a whole, and agricultural conditions generally in the prairie provinces. The acreage under cultivation has not shewn any increase during the past three years. For the year ending March 31, 1913, there were 10,000 less homestead entries than in 1911. In 1911 the land sales were 19,000,000 acres, while, in 1913 it had fallen to 9,000,000 acres. In 1914 the figures to these matters will, I fear, be less favourable. Further, let me say the number of immi-,	158
grants settling on western lands, has been declining, and we are now face to face with the problem how to procure for the future a substantial quantity of land immigration. It is from Eastern Canada and the United States that furnishes land settlers for the West, the major portion of immigration from Europe including the United Kingdom have for some time past been settling in our towns and cities. Our free lands are pretty well disposed of, and European immigrants, as a rule, are not possessed of sufficient capital to purchase. To-day we find ourselves with an immigration policy that has passed its usefulness and it is unsuitable to our needs because it lacks selection methods. Consequently, I say that without the adoption of some new land immigration policy -we cannot look for any substantial increase in land settlement in the West.
Further, we have the following facts particularly relevant to the wheat industry. It is baiely remunerative, if at all, to the producer, the average cost being at least 55 cents per bushel, and the cost of production is apparently increasing, it is said lj,i per cent since 1909, while marketing ar.d exporting charges have as well increased. These facts are important because a large section of the prairie provinces it is conceded must remain grain producing areas, and not easily convertible into mixed farming lands. Important also because the production costs are important to Canad-', whose exportable surplus is large and must consequently meet export prices.
It is to be remembered also that we have tremendous areas not yet devoted to grain growing, which must, if utilized, and if we are to make the desired progress, double and quadruple our production, and that is only possible if the costs of producing are reasonable and the markets available. The production costs and the markets for our western wheat is therefore of vital importance, and always worthy of the most careful consideration. It is true that we usually proceed upon the assumption that our wheat production is to continue to increase greatly, and many at least, presume that markets are awaiting not only our. present productions, but any anticipated increases as well. Now, a>-e we reasonably sure of such markets and under what conditions are any of the world's markets open to us ? Let me present to the House some considerations respecting markets.
Our important wheat market to-day is the United Kingdom. In 1913 the value of our total wheat exports was $88,608,000,



of which the United Kingdom took $74,-
978,000	or over 88 per cent. In the event of an increased production is it sufficiently capacious to consume any considerable proportion of the same ?
The United Kingdom imports about 200,000,000 bushels of wheat, of which to-day Canada supplies about one-fifth, British India one-fifth, Australia one-tenth, the United States one-fifth, and the Argentine one-seventh. While the volume of our exports have grown in the last 15 years, so has that of foreign countries. Two facts should be here noted, namely, that the domestic consumption of the United Kingdom is an almost constant quantity, and that she will continue to buy from all exporting countries of the world which offer the most favourable prices, and particularly those with whom she has an export trade and of which she is creditor nation. It is therefore clear that our only hope of increasing our exports of wheat and wheat flour substantially to the United Kingdom, is by displacing foreign wheat by advantages in quality and price. It is a fact that at present prices the growing of wheat is not very remunerative when in competition with other export wheat, consequently, the price at which we can produce and sell is of manifest importance to Canada.
Now, let us consider the United Kingdom as a market for wheat exported in the form of flour. In 1913 our total exports of flour was 4,478,061 barrels of which 2,880,167 barrels were taken by the United Kingdom, or nearly sixty-five per cent, and the total consumption of flour of the United Kingdom is about 35,000,000 barrels. Will our exports of flour to the United Kingdom increase substantially? I do not think so, because her millers are to-day our strongest competitors. The British miller buys the export wheat of the world and consequently it is cheap. Britain will continue to buy foreign wheat to employ her ships and in payment of interest upon her foreign investments. Again the British miller mixes his wheat, and the British consumer likes the resultant of the mixed product, and consequently the British miller has an advantage over the Canadian miller in buying the variety of raw material.
It is true that Canadian wheat is well regarded for flour purposes because of its strength in gluten, but the United States, Russia and Argentina grow a wheat also strong in gluten, which the British miller buys, consequently in quality of flour required for the United Kingdom we meet strong competition from the British miller.

Again the most modern mills of the world are now found on the docks in Great Britain, and they probably produce flour as cheaply, if not more cheaply, than any country of the world. Newspapers recently reported that a Scotch mill recently exported flour to the United States.
Has the hon. gentleman the figures showing the amount of wheat the United States exports to Great Britain?

No, I have not these figures. Let me continue. I saw in a Canadian paper last week, the statement that soon Canada will supply the United Kingdom with flour. The conditions rather indicate the fact that we will be sorely pressed to hold what we have, unless we can undersell the British miller. The United States miller doubtless thought the same at one time. In 1906 the United States sold to the United Kingdom 10,152,770 cwt. of flour, in 1913 it was 6,157,644 cwts., and it is said that so keenly do American millers find British competition that they are largely withdrawing their selling organizations. And why? There are, I suppose, many contributing causes, hut chiefly the high cost of producing wheat there, and I believe it is even greater than in Canada, unremunerative prices obtained, whether in the form of wheat or wheat flour, in competition with other wheat growing countries and the ~ British miller. To-day we have a milling capacity of over 30,000,000 barrels per year, with an actual production of 15,000,000 barrels, and a domestic consumption of say
10,000,000 barrels, and I ask you, while we talk glibly of increasing our wheat and flour production, where are we going to obtain the market, the consumers?
We have the opportunity, if we want to accept it, of free entry into the markets of the United States, of wheat and flour. Is it worth accepting? The man who produces the wheat is apparently anxious to accept the offer. The Canadian miller objects and the Government objects also or at least it sustains the objection of the Canadian millers. Is his objection just or sound? Our millers are labouring under the mistake that Great Britain will largely absorb our flour exports no matter to what dimensions it grows. Facts rather prove this is an hallucination of the Canadian miller. If it is expected that our exportable surplus of flour is to grow, and it should, our millers should be more alarmed over the competition of the British miller than that of the United States miller, I understand that our miller has requested an ocean steamship service

specially .subsidized for flour exports. This would be a discrimination that- is unnecessary, and would, I think, prove futile, as it has whenever tried. I think if our millers devoted the same energy in utilizing the advantages they possess and in fighting for markets close by, that would consume even the milling capacity we now have, thus reducing the cost of production per unit, it would be found .more profitable to themselves and advantageous to their country than .persistent solicitations for Government favours which I venture to believe would not be helpful. Surely it is clear that we do need other markets for wheat and flour, and it is equally as reasonable a proposition that to ensure this we must do everything to make it possible to produce more cheaply
We can have an additional market. The United States market is open to us. The decision rests with the Government of Canada. The sooner we accept this market the sooner will we there establish ourselves and displace American grown wheat and flour. There would be another .set of mills grinding our wheat. It would enable our millers to grind more steadily and thus more cheaply because our milling capacity would be in use. The problem of the 'Canadian miller is the lack of stomachs to consume flour and cattle to consume offal. The British market is not the panacea nor are ocean freight rates the cause. We want a readjustment of tariff taxation to enable cheaper production. This can be done without any injury to Canadian interests, and it should be done. This matter' should have had the sympathetic consideration of the Government at this session. Wheat should have been placed upon the free list to afford an additional market and other tariff adjustments should have been enacted to encourage all productions in order to render more effective our position with competitors, and particularly for the producers of the prairie provinces where conditions are not too healthy.
Yesterday the Minister of Finance urged as a reason why it was not advisable to put wheat upon, the free list, that it would withdraw traffic from our transcontinental railway lines, which were specially constructed with the view, and in the hope, that our exports would travel east and west thus affording these railways profitable long haul traffic. I wonder if the Minister of Finance was in earnest in propounding that idea? During the campaign of 1911, I often wondered if any man in ,	158i
the Conservative party was really sincere . when he said that free wheat between. Canada and the United States would be inadvisable, because it would destroy the east and west-bound railway traffic, and consequently injure our railways. That, in my opinion, is the most absurd proposition ever propounded. If it be true that the Canadian, railways are at 'the mercy of the United States Government, then the United States Government can withdraw the tariff upon wheat any day and destroy our railway systems. Hon. gentlemen opposite say: why do you want the American market; Canadian wheat will not go there? If that be true, then Canadian wheat will continue to go over the Canadian railways, and the Canadian railways will not be hurt. Hon. gentlemen opposite further say: the price of wheat to Canadian producers, will not be increased by its free admission to the American market. I do not think it is important either to deny or to affirm that contention, but if American wheat is not higher in. price than Canadian wheat, then Canadian wheat will not go to the United States in great quantities and again railway interests will not be hurt. But I go father, and I take the position that there is no reason for imagining that we cannot export to other foreign countries the amount of wheat we are now exporting, and ship it over Canadian railways, while at the same time sell wheat to the United States. Surely the export of our wheat to the United States i.3 not going to destroy our export wheat trade with the other countries of the world. Carry it to the most absurd conclusion the human mind can imagine, and suppose that all our wheat went to the .United .States and none went abroad over the Canadian railway systems, would that hurt the Canadian railways?
I doubt it very much, and I challenge the hon. member for St. Antoine to make good his position, if I understand him to controvert the position which I am now taking. The purchasing power of the people of the Canadian West would be all the greater if they were selling their wheat in the United States alone and not anywhere else in the world, and they would only do it if they were doing it to a greater advantage than by selling their wheat elsewhere. Consequently, the purchasing power of the producer would be increased, and the imports of the West would be much greater. It would mean a higher grade of railway traffic, and the net

result would be that the Canadian railways would be better off than in hauling low grade traffic such as wheat. But I am taking an impossible and absurd position, one that cannot happen for many years. Whether we have free trade with the United States on wheat and wheat flour or not, will not in the slightest degree affect our present export trade with other countries. In fact, there is no reason why we might not have a trade with the United States in wheat to a greater or less extent, while our export trade with other countries would go on increasing, thus giving more business to the Canadian railways than they have now; and even when the Hudson Bay railway, that doubtful project, is completed, there is no reason why any shipments of wheat which can be shipped through Hudson bay should affect the railways of this country, because in a few years we should have such an export of grain from this country that it would tax every system of transportation we have to handle it.
But I want to urge upon hon. gentlemen opposite that peculiar conditions prevail in the West, and I feel that the Government are not properly seized of the actual facts. I believe that at this moment it will be in the interest of Canada, east and west, of the Canadian producer of wheat, of the Canadian miller, and of the Canadian consumer, to place wheat upon the free list, and consequently we upon this side of the House regret that the Government has seen fit not to place wheat upon the free list.
I would go further, because in the Budget debate it is not necessary that we should tonflne our discussion merely to matters of finance and of tariffs. .We should discuss generally the condition of our country. I would not limit the efforts of Government policy and Government action in dealing with problems of the West to the question of tariff alone. I believe we have reached the time when we should extend more direct and practical aid to agriculture, with special adaptation to the peculiar problems confronting the pioneer farmers of the three prairie provinces. They should be helped in other and more direct and practical ways which would produce immediate, permanent and profitable results. I am sure that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House are in favour of any policy which will extend some aid of a practical nature to the people of the West, who are endeavouring under difficult circumstances to produce from the soil wealth which this

country needs. From the West for many years in the future must come the exports of natural products which alone will pay for the imports of this country.
Hon. gentlemen opposite speak a great deal about the new agricultural policy, which means an expenditure of a million dollars a year. I congratulate the Government upon doing that much, but after all it is not very much. I do not know that it justifies a great volume of boasting, or that it indicates a great deal of careful study or reflection upon the actual agricultural conditions of this country. We have reached a stage in this country when we should do more for agricultural interests, and we would do so if we realized more clearly and accurately the tremendous part agriculture plays in the business and prosperity of this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite speak about the so-called National Policy being beneficial to agriculture. The policy of the present Government in respect to agriculture generally, but in reference particularly to the question which I have just been debating, namely, the wheat tariff, is not designed in the interest of the agricultural producer.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Bill No. 149, for the relief of Harry Cracroft Pugh.-Mr. Douglas.

At six o'clock I was urging that, in view of the prevailing conditions in the Northwest provinces, in addition to encouragement in the way of possible tariff revision, we should not hesitate to afford them aid that would apply directly and practically to the needs of that country and to the peculiar difficulties confronting the farmers of that section. I have been informed since six o'clock, that a decision has been made by the Board of Railway Commissioners in the way of reduction of railway freight rates which will mean a great deal to those provinces, particularly to Saskatchewan and Alberta. I am sure this will be received with much gratification by all citizens of Canada, and particularly by those most directly affected. The Railway Board is a

creation of the late Administration, and the measure which created them was one of the acts of that Government to which hon. members on this side of the House always point with a great deal of pride and satisfaction. The Railway Board is a body which has rendered very important service to Canada, and if in the determination of the issue of railway freights which has been before them, they have succeeded in effecting such reduction as will prove an important factor in the interest of the people of the western provinces, then the Act establishing that commission has been still further justified.
There is just one more matter I propose discussing before concluding my remarks, and that is the question of tariff policy respecting food products. We had very little from the Minister of Finance on that subject yesterday; in fact, nothing. I was somewhat surprised by this omission, because the question of the cost of living is of extraordinary importance and is receiving very serious consideration on the part of all classes of people. I think, further, that it is a condition of affairs that calls for practical, serious consideration on the part of the Government. I do not propose to engage in a detailed discussion of the high cost of living, or of what remedy should be applied by way of tariff amendments. I rather purpose asserting some general principles in respect of this question. The high cost of living, the phenomenal increase in the prices of the actual necessities of life, requires no proof or evidence from me. The prices of articles which are the actual necessities of life, particularly of foodstuffs, have been constantly rising for years, until to-day the wage-earners and the small salaried classes are facing the lowering of the living standard, or they are obliged to forego many of the actual necessities of life and cease to enjoy many of the advantages which hitherto they have enjoyed. In this respect, phenomenal conditions prevail throughout the world, conditions intensely interesting, and deemed of sufficient importance by all countries to receive the most thorough and careful consideration by their best-trainea economists. Now, I am not going to assert that the Government is entirely responsible for the prevailing high cost of living so called. For this phenomenon many causes are assigned, but I do not propose to enumerate or discuss them. Some probably are beyond our control, while the effects of some may be at least minimized if not removed. I do not propose either to
give any comparative statement of prices. This is too well known. Neither do I propose discussing any lengthy list of articles, the prices of which are considered high. However, I wish to discuss very briefly the matter of the prices of foodstuffs, and to suggest what we should do in the circumstances.
To-day most foodstuffs are taxed or subject to duty, and this undoubtedly contributes to the cost. The tariff duties must affect the prices of foodstuffs, else no one would object to their removal, and they would never have been established. Is this not right? Does there exist any real justification for the continuance of the imposition of duties upon staple foodstuffs, in view of the existing prices, and in view of the fact that it apparently carries no real advantage to the producer? Let us consider a few articles. Take the matter of meats, so essential a foodstuff. What is the world-wide condition? The world is hardly producing sufficient for its needs. That is true of Canada to-day. Our production of live-stock is declining, and, this being an important consideration, I desire to give the House some figures bearing upon this point, as helping to an intelligent consideration of the question. Probably. In this country to-day, particularly at certain seasons of the year, many of our people are compelled to abstain from purchasing some of these articles by reason of the cost. If we have to import these articles why not let those who require them have free of duty taxation if possible. I am simply asserting that policy as a general principle. There may be exceptions to it which I shall discuss later.
Does the hon. gentleman argue that the list of foodstuffs last mentioned should be admitted to this country free of duty?
I am going to argue that in a moment.
Will the hon. gentleman not answer me now?

Yes. My .position is this: Staple food products, as a general rule, should be admitted into this country free of duty unless for very good and substantial reasons. In formulating and readjusting a tariff upon foodstuffs the guiding principle should be to make foodstuffs free of duty. The necessities of revenue would of course be a natural exception to that view.
To-day -we are in receipt of ample revenue, tout one can easily conceive that almost at any time the Government might require further revenue. I do not mean to assert that I would carry this principle so far as to say that such imports should not be taxable for purposes of revenue.
I go a little farther and perhaps this is what my hon. friend wishes me to discuss. I think the maintenance of a tariff in this country upon foodstuffs was more defensible for the purposes of retaliation against our neighbour than upon other grounds. I do not accept it as a fact that tariff imposts upon agricultural produce imports into this country have been beneficial to the producers. I assert that, as a general principle. I would think it only fair that any government, in taking into consideration the readjustment of the tariff upon foodstuffs, while guided mainly by the principle of giving the consumers untaxed foodstuffs, should take into consideration the question of how -such articles, when imported into a foreign country from Canada, are treated in the way of tariff duties. I am, willing to concede that that is a fair matter for consideration, but as a general principle I say that staple food products might well be admitted into this country free of duty.
To-day we are trying to drive Canadian trade across a continent 3,000 miles: with a dead section intervening between the West and the East. It is an ambitious scheme on the part of Canadians. It is perhaps in many respects deserving of commendation. We have all done our part to develop trade between the eastern and western parts of Canada, as well as intexprovincial trade, but in a country extending from ocean to ocean it is not sound, economically, and I deny its justice, to be endeavouring to force traffic and trade in foodstuffs particularly across a continent some 2,500 or
3,000	miles in extent. It is unnatural, and economically wasteful. If the Canadian Northwest develops its agricultural productions in the next few years, as it should, it will become the strong competitor of the farmer of Ontario, Quebec, and the Maritime provinces. It will not he the competitor of the farmer in the United States.

We will have the same condition of affairs that prevailed in the United States some years ago. When the western states [DOT]were heavy exporters they were able to dispose heavily of their products in the eastern -states with the result that the eastern farmer felt the competition. That *will be the result in this country if the West develops in the production of agricultural commodities as I believe and hope it "will. It will be to the advantage of the eastern farmer, therefore, if the farmer of the West has an outlet in the western or middle western states so that there he may find a consuming market for his surplus products. It apparently will happen in this country that while we are exporters of certain products, such as bacon, for instance, where our exports are much larger than the quantity imported, we can still have an import trade to the advantage of the consumer.
It is not wise to say that we should consider only the interests of the producer of agricultural commodities, for we must remember that we have a large number of consumers, in fact, numerically greater than the producers to-day in Canada. It is not fair or just to the consumer to say that in all cases in respect to foodstuffs he must accept and purchase from the Canadian producer regardless of circumstances, or pay the import duty.
Peculiar economic conditions prevail today respecting the price of the real necessities of life throughout the country and we must take them into consideration else we cannot deal logically or in a businesslike way with the problem that I aim now attempting to discuss. The situation today is altogether different from what it was some years ago. A new set of facts and conditions confronts us and it is our duty,
' in providing a remedy and in seeking some alleviation of present conditions on behalf of the consumer, to study the actual facts and conditions so that we may discuss the remedy in an intelligent manner. The effect of a tariff to-day is not what it was a few years ago. The same is true of the United States and of all the world. Trade has become internationalized, and many duties exist upon imports which do not affect the quantity of the imports hr the price of the article or articles imported. I believe that if the duty ware removed from some articles it would not vary in one iota the quantity of imports of such articles, nor perhaps would it affect the price. There are combinations of trade between some
producers, between transportation systems, and between middlemen that absolutely nullify the effect and intention of a tariff. For that reason I say that the question of tariffs to-day must he considered in the light of new conditions. This, I think, was well expressed in the following annual crop report of the Department of Agriculture of the United States issued January, 1914:
The long line of distributors and middlemen between the farmer and consumer are in a position to take advantage of the market and to a certain extent control the market in botli directions, because they are better organized to keep informed of crop and market conditions and to act more promptly than either farmers or consumers, who are not organized and as individuals are helpless.
The high prices paid by consumers, ranging from 5 to nearly 500 per cent in some cases more than the farmer received, indicate that there is plenty of room for lowering the cost of farm products to consumers and at the same time largely increase the cash income per farm without increasing farm production.
This, Sir, is, I believe, an actual fact in the working out of things to-day. When one discusses the removal or reduction of tariffs upon agricultural products, it does not follow that the producer will be affected in the least, although it may operate to the disadvantage of the middleman or possibly some transportation system. I do not think it is the opinion of many farmers or producers of foodstuffs, that the tariff now existing is in their interest. I do Pot say that statement is not subject to some exception, because I dare say there are some producers of certain agricultural foodstuffs, who would contend, and perhaps with some measure of success, that a tariff was of some advantage to them. But generally speaking, the producer does not get the advantage of any substantial proportion of the price paid today by the consumers of staple foodstuffs, as has been proven time and again in many instances in Canada and the United States. There are some producers of foodstuffs in this country, who are no, asserting that the removal or reduction of duties upon foodstuffs will operate as an injury to him. A memorial from the Dominion Council of Agriculture was presented to this Government in December last, and in that memorial I find these words:
We ask that all foodstuffs he placed on the free list, as we believe that the taxing of foodstuffs is a crime against humanity.
Who said that?

The Dominion Council
of Agriculture represents a very large body

of the producers of agricultural products in the province of Ontario, and of the West. I be-lieve that very shortly after this memorial was presented to the Government, a countermemorial was presented by another delegation from the province of Ontario. Am I right in that?
The members of the first delegation were agriculturists; the members of the second delegation were farmers.

I think the truth is that the first delegation was composed of farmers and the second was composed of politicians. It appeared that way to me at least. The second delegation appear to me to hav<-been staged to counteract the representations of the former delegation or memorial. I do not know whether the first one was or not; at all events, they were quite frank.
If my hon. friend will excuse me, I would like to say that that statement is not in accordance with fact.
Which statement ?
The statement that the delegation was engineered and brought down here for a purpose.
Though I am always glad to accept the word of the Minister of Public Works, I must say that it had to me that appearance.
The farmers of Ontario, who came here on the 21st of December, 1911, did not say they wanted free wheat.
I do not know that the hon. gentlemen opposite would be glad to submit that issue once again to the farmers of Ontario.
South Bruce.

The question of the
high cost of living and of placing foodstuffs on the free list, subject to the possible exceptions and considerations I have mentioned, deserves a more complete argument than I intend to make to-night. When I commenced to speak upon this point, it was my intention merely to assert some general facts and principles in connection with the question.
The Minister of Finance stated yesterday that free food means free trade. Surely that is an untenable proposition. Where does the Minister of Finance get authority for that view? He did not endeavour to substantiate it, and I doubt his ability, or that of any other hon. gentleman, to do so. You may resort to history, to experi-
ence, or to facts, but you will fail to find anything which would support the proposition of the Minister of Finance, that free food means free trade. The theory that free food means free trade is a protectionist doctrine. It is the idea merely of those who try to make the farmer believe he is a beneficary of the protection given to others. This idea I thought was long ago discarded.
We do not want to discard it.

I suppose the .Minister of Public Works is right in saying that he and his friends do not want to discard protective duties, and therefore they take refuge in the absurd doctrine that free food means free trade. He wants food to support his protective tariff duties. When protection was first established in Canada and in the United States, it was said to be for the aid of infant industries; but it is obvious that argument could not last forever, and it has been abandoned. The old established industry seems to want protection as much as the industry started but yesterday.
In the United States they abandoned that thirty years ago; and when they did so, what did they take up? They said it increased the wages of labour. That argument was urged for a period, but it has also been abandoned. Nobody urges that to-day. Experience has proved that it cannot be established as a fact., Up to the year of 1890 or thereabouts there was no such thing as protection for the farmer in the United States tariff. It was the McKinley tariff Bill which imposed upon agricultural products a tariff for protection purposes. It was in the time of McKinley that we first heard the campaign of protection for the farmers. He was placing the responsibility of the continuance of the high protective tariff upon the farmer, hut he really intended it for other classes. Even the protectionist, I thought, had abandoned the justification of the tariff upon the ground that it is necessary for the farmer's interest. He has resorted to another argument, namely, that there should be a tariff to equalize the aifference in the cost of production in. the home country and in the importing country. That is the doctrine put forward today in the United States in support of the policy of protection. That was the doctrine held by the Minister of Finance last session or the session before when he introduced his Tariff Commission Bill. That was his justification for it. He never then

urged that-, if you have free foodstuffs, you will have free trade. He did not then mean to suggest that it costs more to produce foodstuff in this country than it does in the United States, and that it was necessary to determine the precise difference by a tariff commission. Therefore, I say that the proposition that the placing of foodstuffs upon the free list necessarily means the adoption of free trade, is untenable and absurd. I do not propose pursuing my argument further upon this point.
In conclusion, considering the peculiar economic conditions - prevailing tc-day, considering the high cost of living which presses iSorely upon many classes of our people, considering the extremely high prices of the actual necessities of life, particularly foodstuffs, considering the fact that the producer of foodstuffs apparently receives little if any advantage from the Canadian tariff to-day imposed upon foodstuffs, I ask: have we not reached that stage when we might, for the benefit of the consumer, place foodstuffs upon the free list? That is the position which we upon this side of the House take, and I think the position is sound as a general principle. I believe we have the human side at least of the issue. Hon. gentlemen opposite say we must continue it upon foodstuffs or the whole fabric of our tariff will fall. That position is unsound; and the Min9 p.m. ister of Finance, in making his tariff changes yesterday, demonstrated to some degree at least that that doctrine was unsound, because he made decreases as well as increases, in the tariff rates, and in some instances he placed articles upon the free list.
Economically our position upon this question is sound. I believe it is in the interest of both the producer and consumer, I submit that the Government should immediately take into consideration the matter of taxation upon foodstuffs in this country. If the Minister of Finance desires to adhere to the position- that he asserted yesterday, that he will not consider the demand of the Canadian consumer for the remission of taxation upon foodstuffs, if he will continue to adhere to the position that he will not consider the revision of the tariff upon foodstuffs, we are satisfied to meet hon. gentlemen opposite before the people of this country upon the issue. We are ready to meet them at Philippi upon that policy.

Mr. Speaker, it has fallen upon me to endeavour to deal with some of the arguments laid before this House by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. E. Maclean). It is not my intention to occupy the time of the House for a period of four hours, but I shall endeavour in a few moments, as speedily as I can-for I am a man of rather few words-to deal with some points at least which the junior member for Halifax has made, and which I think should not pass unchallenged.
In his opening remarks he made two observations, one of which I can re-echo, the other of which I would take issue with him upon. He expressed the hope that the present depression was only temporary, and that full prosperity would very speedily arrive. While hardly admitting that Canada to-day is not fully prosperous, I shall still be quite prepared to'join with him in hoping that greater prosperity may come to her in the near future.
When the junior member for Halifax characterizes the remarks made in this House yesterday by the hon. Minister of Finance as being apologetic and fearful, I confess that I cannot share his views. As near as we could judge from this side of the House-and the hon. Minister of Finance must have presented an altogether different appearance from the other side, if the remarks of the junior member for Halifax hold goodr-the Minister of1 Finance seemed full of optimism, vigour and determination-and, I trust, of good health to carry to a successful issue those projects which he brought forward. The junior member for Halifax laboured long and arduously	all afternoon	in	anendeavour to convict the hon. Minister of Finance of some wrongdoing. I f-eel very much like letting the verdict go as 'not proven.'	I do not think	the	hon.gentleman has	brought home	in	hiscriticism anything very serious	with	reference to the policy of the Government or of the Minister of Finance. And yet, I am hardly willing to even let him have the -benefit of such a verdict, because I believe that the teeling of this House is that the Minister of Finance, in dealing . with this question and with his own record, has been, if anything, over modest, as is his wont, and has not taken to himself the full meed of praise to which he is certainly entitled. After three years of successful -administration there begin to emerge a sufficient number of facts and figures to make comparison with previous
administrations possible; and I propose to take a few moments to emphasize some of the points which seem to me worthy of being spoken of and being again emphasized in the remarks of the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance is no pessimist; he is a conservative optimist. He sees things as they are, and he does not see shadows where shadows do not lie; and 1 think he is prepared to fearlessly face the future in the belief that Canada will be able to continue her forward and prosperous career. We all admit that there are periods of temporary depression; we ail admit that a new country goes ahead very much like the kangaroo, by long leaps with occasional rests between. We ail admit that progress cannot be measured in absolute equality year after year, that there are years when we recuperate, and years when we expand with such rapidity that we hardly know ourselves as we grow. One has only to look out upon the spectacle which nature gives us here, and will give us in the next few weeks. There are days when the buds open rapidly, when we can almost see things grow; there are other days when the winds are cold and the sun is hidden, when for several days it does not seem as if there was any progress made m growing vegetation. But we all know that spring and summer will come, that the bud will appear and the leaf and flower and fruit. And so do we believe it will be with Canada, that, though there may be days, though there may be years, when progress is not quite so rapid as in others, yet we are certain that the growth and expansion which we now note is but begun.
Now, the year 1912-13 has already been referred to and was referred to by the Minister of Finance one year ago. It may almost be termed ancient history. And yet the figures were not fully before us -a year ago, but are now recorded in a blue book. This being always the istate of affairs, it is customary, when the Budget Speech is made, to deal with two years instead of one. That the year was wisely administered, we all admit, that was the year when the Finance Minister, looking out upon the world-and the Finance Minister of Canada must consider conditions in every part of the world-anr seeing dark clouds gathering, with war threatening in certain quarters, made preparations, as he wisely should, 
to meet this storm when it should gather, to offset a depression which might come. For, as we all know, Canada and the rest of the world are so intimately linked together that no part of the world can suffer in nonproductiveness without all the world suffering in consequence; and when war breaks out in one part of the world we, like all other parts of the world, feel the results of it even in this peaceful and prosperous country of ours. So the Finance Minister exercised caution to such an extent that out of the revenues of that year 1912-13 after meeting all the running expenses, everything that could be properly charged to consolidated revenue account, he had. no less than $56,630,000 to the good. And he took that sum, as lie wisely should, and invested it-invested it in permanent public works, to the extent of over $32,400,000, works which are, for the most part productive, and he invested the balance in the reduction of the debt. So, in that year, our public debt was decreased by $25,617,000. In other words, having a revenue of $3, he spent $2 in current expenses and laid $1 away partly in supplying revenue producing works and partly in liquidating our indebtedness to the world. Could anything be more wise or more conservative than that? Can any year in the history of Canada show a better record than that?
And what had been foreseen with wise foresight by the Finance Minister came to pass. The year from which we have just emerged 1913-14 was not a year of the greatest prosperity such as Canada sometimes sees; it has been a year in which there were trying conditions, and we were able to meet those conditions and overcome them very largely because of the wise foresight exercised in the administration of our affairs for the previous year.
We have before us, the approximate figures for the year 1913-14. They are not complete, but they will serve for the purposes for which we wish to use them. We find that we have had a revenue on consolidated fund account of $163,000,000. The diminution was due mainly to a falling off in customs duties, which is no cause for special alarm, for it means that importations have not been quite as great as usual, and that means that there has been a general reduction of stocks held by our leading firms and that their renewals of these stocks have been more or less cautious owing to the falling off in the demand of the country. But we are perfectly sure, since the quantity of goods that must

be consumed in Canada does not greatly vary year by year except as it expands with out increasing population, we may be sure that in a very short time out customs revenue wiill again expand, because stocks throughout Canada are low and must be increased. So, there is no reason to expect a serious falling off in revenue within the next few years.
Now, the year 1913-14 which by the junior member for Halifax has been subjected to much criticism, will, I think, bear most minute scrutiny and careful examination. In that year our revenue was $163,000,000. We expended on current expenses chargeable to consolidated fund $126,500,000. In other words, the balance to the good after paying running expenses, was $36,500,000 That was not enough, says the junior member for Halifax, to pay all capital demands. That I admit. Nor do I lay it down as a rule that enough should annually be collected to pay all capital demands. It has always been the custom in new countries-dominions, provinces, cities -when a great public work was undertaken which would be for the benefit of generations yet to come, that a portion at least of that expense should be borne by those who eventually will profit by it. And so when a great capital expenditure is made it is customary that a portion of the required amount shall be paid, for by money borrowed and the carrying of sinking fund and interest shall not be merely upon the shoulders of the present generation, but upon the shoulders of those who may come alter and are likely to enjoy the benefits. So, I would not lay it down as a rule, to be deviated from never that all the money spent on capital account must be taken from the annual taxation of the people, and must be paid for year by year. A reasonable amount may each year be borrowed, and, provided it is invested carefully so that we get one hundred cents on the dollar in productive enterprises, there can be no criticism of this course as being bad finance. But there are a good many of the accounts that bad to be paid in the last year for which this Government is not at all responsible. We beard more than once, to quote the classical phrase of the Minister of Finance, that it is the hereditas damnosa which has taken away our apparently surplus revenue. Let us see just what are the reasons why this year also we did not reduce the public debt. In the first place, we had to provide for a certain number of public works. We could not bring them suddenly to an end. There is construction
in various parts of Canada-work on the Intercolonial, the canals, the public building's, harbour improvements- all had to go on, and upwards of $19,000,000 was spent in that way which it would have been difficult if not dangerous to have curtailed. Then, let us also remember that during the last year we had to meet $12,600,000 for the National Transcontinental railway; we had to meet $2,800,000 for the Quebec bridge, and between one and a half and two million dollars for the Hudson Bay railway. Let me in all fairness ask members of this House which of these three projects are the ministers now in power responsible for; and if that $17,000,000 has to be provided for this year, can it be said that it is due to the extravagance of this Administration, when all these projects were originated before this party came into power?
But the feature of the expenditure last year which strikes one most forcibly, although it was passed over very lightly indeed by the junior member for Halifax, was the great sum that was required to be paid out in railway subsidies. Railway subsidies have been paid in this country for the last thirty or forty years. If you look back over the list of expenditures you will see that in the twenty-nine years which end with 1913 there has been paid out for railway subsidies $48,430,187. It is to be presumed that this resulted in the construction of many lines of railway. That is an average of a little over one and a half millions a year, and never before in a single year has the amount exceeded $5,000,000. How much was it last year? I wonder if the members of this House, I wonder if you, Mr. Speaker, have any idea of the sums that were expended during the year 1913-14 in railway subsidies? They reached the enormous sum of $19,036,236, almost enough to account for the entire addition to the debt that has taken place during the last year. Now, we admit that the present Government is to some extent responsible for expenditures on capital account, which I have totalled at $19,000,000. We admit that they may be held responsible because they would not allow great works to cease in connection with the National Transcontinental railway, the Quebec bridge and the Hudson Bay railway. But for these railway subsidies you have only to look back at the legislation to find that, with one exception, I think, they are not primarily chargeable to the present Government. Some of

thes-e railway subsidies have run away with very large sums of money. If, for example, you total what was paid last year to the Canadian Northern Pacific, the Canadian Northern]	Alberta;	the Canadian
Northern Ontario, you will find that they took $14,301,000, and every one of the original Acts was passed in 1910 or 191Lamd were part of thie hered'itas darrmosa which has fallen upon this Government. And recent events demonstrate, I think clearly, that the stand which the present Prime Minister took when in 1911 the former Government brought into this House a measure for the building of the Canadian Northern Ontario railroad, has been more than justified by the events. He asked at that time some very pertinent questions as to whether there was room for a third transcontinental railway at the present time, and he expressed a good deal of doubt in that respect. I am sure that the doubt he then expressed has become firmly fixed in the minds of many people to-day. How do you get railway competition? Not always by building railroads. It is possible to build so many railroads that you cannot get railroad competition. When you have two railroads serving a district where there is not quite enough traffic for both but pretty nearly, you get competition and a reduction of rates. Where you have three railroads serving a district where there is not enough traffic for two, you get a combine and a general keeping up of rates, or one or two of the railways go under the hammer. So this country, I think, has frequently been led away with the idea that it was always justifiable to build a railway, always justifiable to subsidize a railway, always justifiable to give a bond guarantee to a railway, and yet it may happen that we in Canada are considerably anticipating our railroad needs and that it becomes necessary for us often times to take money, that we need for other things far more, to carry out the promises of a previous Administration.
But to come hack to our financial discussion for a moment, I want to congratulate the Finance Minister on his foresight, as I have already said, in preparing for this year 1913-14. Many demands were made upon him and yet the year has a showing of which he need not in any way be ashamed. True, he had the disagreeable task of frequently refusing to lend the aid of the Government to propositions supported by many a member, propositions which were unquestionably valuable but which will have to stand over becruse of other 
needs that must be met. Well the clouds are clearing and the time will come, I trust, when we shall be free from the inheritance that has been left us and be able once again, on our own initiative, to decide wlrat shall be done with the money which the taxpayers contribute. I -said that the Finance Minister, seeing that hard times were coming, made preparation by laying aside one dollar out of every three that came into his hands 'in 1912-13. His predecessor, the Finance Minister of some years ago, has been referred to to-night and has been held up as a shining example, yet I hardly think if our present Finance Minister had followed his example, he would have found himself in the enviable position in which he is to-day. Five years ago there was one of these cycles of depression. 1907-8 had been a bumper year. The revenues had reached nearly $100,000,000. Hon. members used to brag about that. The actual figures were $96,000,000, and yet in that year, with $96,000,000 of revenue there was an over Expenditure of $11,000,000, all kinds added together. In that year there were ominous signs of troubles to come. Did the Finance Minister of that day put on the brakes? No, there were threatenings of stringency, and yet full steam ahead was the watchword of the Government at that time. In 1908-09 the revenues fell, as they were expected to fall, by $11,000,000, to $85,000,000. The total expenditure of that year was $131,000,000, and the net result was that we added $46,000,000 to the net- debt of Canada in a single year. Oh, yes, the former Finance Minister did put on the brakes, but he did it one year too late. He could not do it in 1908, for obvious reasons.
The junior member for Halifax indulged in a comparison of records. We are quite willing to submit to such comparisons. We have only three years that we can point to as having held the reins of power, while our predecessors had between fifteen and sixteen years, but we are quite willing to compare our three with their fifteen or sixteen. Turn, for example, to the net debt. In 1896, when the Conservatives went out of power, the net debt of Canada was $258,497,000. In 1911, when the Conservatives came into pow'er, it stood at $340,042,000; it had increased in the sixteen years of Liberal rule by $81,500,000, or at the steady rate of about $5,000,000 a year. I am not seriously objecting to a moderate increase of debt, because, as I previously explained, it is sometimes necessary that capital expenditure should be distributed over a term of years

but I do not like to hear people bragging about what they really have not accomplished, and consequently it becomes necessary to make a comparison of this character. The net debt in 1911 was $340,000,000 odd. The net debt on the 31st of March, 1914. was $333,300,000. In other words, the previous Government added $81,500,000 to the debt in sixteen years while the present Government in three years have not only not added a dollar, but they have reduced the debt by $6,750,000-and that although they have put $125,000,000 into enterprises that are usually chargeable to capital account- at least, not chargeable to consolidated fund.
If you take the three years before and the three years after that great event of the 21st of September, 1911-the years 1909, 1910 and 1911 showed an increase in the public debt of $62,000,000, -while the years 1912, 1913 and 1914 showed a decrease in the public debt of $6,750,000. It will therefore be seen that we are in a better position by nearly $69,000,000 when you compare the three years previous to September, 1911, -and the three years that followed.
We all remember how the changes used to be rung in this Chamber on the annual surpluses Somehow or other, however much might be added to the public debt it was always stated that there was a surplus at the end of the year and the previous Administration prided themselves on that. We used to criticise the method by which it was calculated, and perhaps we should criticse it even now, but at least we will call it by its right name and only use it for purposes of comparison. What do we find in this matter of so-called surpluses; because what used to be regarded as a surplus was the amount of money you had left after you took the total revenue and deducted therefrom the current expenses ot what was chargeable to consolidated fund. That is what was called a surplus even although it might be wiped out two or three times over in a year by capital account. Taking the fifteen years from 1896 to 1911 we find that these much vaunted surpluses aggregate $167,000,000. Although the debt had grown $81,500,000 in that time, the claim was always made in this House that there was an annual surplus. Using the same method of comparison we find that the first year after this Administration came into power there was a surplus of $37,946,000; in the second year a surplus of $56,630,000, and in the third year, which
lias just passed, a surplus of $35,000,000, or somewhere around that figure-the figures are not yet complete. In other words, the surpluses during the last three years have totalled $130,000,000, and if we have good luck for one year more, the total surpluses in the lifetime of the present Parliament will he equal to the surpluses of the four Parliaments of the 16 years that preceded it.
Some of our liabilities have been referred to by the hon. gentleman who preceded me, and perhaps it might be well just here to say a word regarding some of the maturing liabilities that have been dealt with in the last two years. It is always a pleasant thing to pay your debts, and when they are paid promptly it is worth while taking credit for it. On the 1st of May, 1912, there were liabilities falling due to the extent of $22,785,000 odd. Of that we were able to redeem 80 per cent in cash and we had only to continue a loan of some $5,440,000. On the 1st of October, 1912, we had $6,010,000 falling due, every dollar of which was paid in cash. On the 1st of October, 1913, we had $8,273,000 falling due, every dollar of which was redeemed in cash; and on the 1st of November, 1913, we had $1,446,500 falling due, all successfully met, and now we are happy to say that for the first five years with the exception of temporary loans there is no more of our funded indebtedness to be dealt with. The Government has come to the end of the woods.
In connection with this indebtedness, an interesting feature came to my notice which perhaps is not really pertinent to this discussion, but which, nevertheless, from an historical point of view at least will be interesting to the House. We paid off last year the last of the old Imperial guaranteed loan. On the 1st of October, 1913, we paid off $8,273,333, the last loan that had the underwriting of the British Government as guaranteeing it in the markets of the world. There was a day when Canada had not the credit she has to-day, and when she could not undertake any great work without first having made very careful preparations as to where the' money was coming from. In those days the lenders of the world were not so ready to give us money on our own face value as they are to-day, and it is interesting to look hack and see -how the Imperial Government stood behind Canada in those early days and made it possible for this country to carry on some of her great works. In 1869 there was $7,300,000 outstanding of imperial guarantee loan at four per cent. In 1874 that had reached $16,000,000; by

1877 it was up to $23,300,000; and in 1885 it stood at $31,633,333. In other words $31,600,000 of the debt of this country was at one time underwritten by the British Parliament. Why was that done? In the first place we find the objects for which the money was used. It was used for. the purchase of Rupert's Land, for Canadian defence loans, for the Canadian Pacific railway, for canal construction, and for other public works which in those earlier days were more than this country could carry upon its own credit. It was not after all, though, a matter so much of credit as it was a matter of saving of interest that really led the British Government to come to our assistance in that respect. That is brought out very clearly by Sir Francis Hincks who in 1872, spoke in the House of Commons as follows:
But if we went into the market for $40,000,000, one half our own, and the other half guaranteed by England, and, with the prestige that England sanctioned our great public improvements, the advantages would be very great, so much so that I am persuaded that under those circumstances we should get our 5 per cent bonds floated at par, and therefore we should be able to float half at 4 per cent and the other half at 5 per cent, or equal to 4J per cent on the whole amount. This would, therefore, make a difference of 1J per cent on the whole amount of $40,000,000, equal to $600,000 a year.
In other words, when Canada found it necessary to borrow $40,000,000 in order to undertake the necessary public works, canals, railroads, and so on, the British Government undertook to guarantee half of that amount in order that half that loan should be floated at four per cent and the other half at five per cent, instead of all being floated at six per cent, bringing about a saving of interest of $600,000 a year. If that had been persisted in, it would have amounted in forty years to upwards of $24,000,000. In other words-and this is the interesting part of it-when our credit was not what it is to-day, the motherland was prepared to help us out and guarantee our loans, even though the money was to be spent in Canada. The mother country was prepared to make it possible for us to borrow in the markets of the world at a rate of interest otherwise impossible, and now the time has come when we have paid off all those loans and we can to-day go into the markets of the world and borrow what we like without the imperial guarantee. Now that that time has come, there has come with it certain responsibilities and duties which this part of the empire, which regards itself as no longer needing a guarantee, should take upon itself.

I regret that as yet it has not shown that it appreciates this fact.
We have been told by the hon. junior member for Halifax that no less than $60,000,000 was borrowed last year. This is held up as a huge sum, as a sum entirely unwarranted, and yet I think if we examine what was done with it we will see, in the first place, that we could not help borrowing and, in the second place, that we used the money well. It was used to meet maturing liabilities to the extent of $10,000,000 (that were unavoidable. We have to meet our debts when they come due. We had to buy Grand Trunk Pacific bonds at par; we bought $11,133,473 worth in 1912-1913, and we bought $12,872,233 worth in 1913-14. We did that to save Canada's credit in the money markets of the world. We thought it better to do so than to have bonds with Canada's guarantee upon them sold over the auction counter at a job lot price.
I was much amused when my hon. friend undertook to point out that an investment of money in Grand Trunk Pacific bonds should not be regarded as an asset. He said:	You should at least take them at
75 cents on the dollar. That does not sound very much like the debate we listened to a little while ago. We certainly believe that the day will come when these bonds will be worth par. We look upon these bonds as securities upon which the full three per cent will be paid, and we hope the day will come when we can dispose of these bonds at par. We have apparently more faith in the Grand Trunk Pacific	project than have our hon.
friends opposite when they say to us: You have taken $23,000,000 of Grand Trunk Pacific bonds that should not count at all as assets because we consider them of very doubtful value. That is the hardest knock that the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific have had in this House, and they have had some hard knocks. Then we had to loan the Grand Trunk Pacific last year $8,500,000. So you see that in these three items that I have mentioned $31,000,000, or more than half of the total of the amount is at once taken up. These items go to increase the gross debt, but they are investments bearing interest, and one of the very interesting matters which hon. gentlemen can verify for themselves is to isee how the percentage that we are getting upon our investments is increasing while the percentage that we
