are paying for our money is decreasing, showing a very satisfactory state of affairs.
My hon. friend entertained us for some time with a denunciation of the high rate of interest that had been paid on certain temporay loans by the Minister of Finance within the last few months. There are times when it is not desirable to go upon the money markets of the world and attempt to float a large loan. If you happen to have liabilities maturing it may be better to finance them as best you can for a new months. Under those circumstances you negotiate a short loan, sometimes for six months and sometimes for a year. The Minister of Finance, just like all other Ministers of Finance in this country, had at times to raise certain temporary loans. We Were told that the discounting of treasury bills at 41 per cent was something that could under no circumstances be justified. Well, you only have to turn back to the Budget speech of Mr. Fielding in 1909, where he gives a table of the loans which up to that time had been issued, and you will find that a 4 per cent loan issued in December, 1908, and good for four years, carried a rate of interest, or what we speak of as the annual effective rate of interest per unit, of .04796 per cent, or 4^ per cent, although the loan just preceding carried an effective rate of interest of .0288 per cent. This proves the fact that the amount of interest that must be paid upon a loan varies very considerably, and it oftentimes happens that for a short loan the Government have to pay rather a high price for the money they get.
These outstanding temporary loans were criticised severely this afternoon, but they are nothing new. It is not as if the making of temporary loans was a crime that had been committed for the first time. Let the hon. gentleman turn up the public accounts and he will see that temporary Loans were quite customary under the previous Administration, and I do not blame them for it. In 1908, when the figures of the year were cast on the 31st March, there were found to be temporary loans outstanding of $9,300,000; in 1909, $13,600,000, and in 1910, $17,033,000. Therefore, the fact that the Minister of Finance of the present day has a loan of $8,500,000 to-day outstanding is nothing for which, I think, he should be blamed to any extent.
I have also been very much interested in the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. A. K.
Maclean) with reference to retrenchment. It seems to me that the subject is out of place at this time. If the speech of my hon. friend had been delivered during the National Transcontinental railway debate a few years earlier, or when the National Transcontinental railway was discussed in the House here a short time ago, it would have been extremely pertinent. I would like to take quotations from that speech and insert them in some of the speeches that were made some years ago in reference to the National Transcontinental railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific, or some of the speeches that were made only a few weeks ago in reference to that extravagant expenditure. But I should like to ask my hon. friend this question. He declared that we should have brought some of these great expenditures to an absolute standstill. He did not realize, or, if he did realize it, he would not have made these observations to the House, that at the beginning of last year very large enterprises in all parts of Canada employing large numbers of men were being rapidly pushed to completion. He did not realize apparently, that it would have been a suicidal act to have brought these great enterprises to a standstill while they were still uncompleted and unproductive. It had become necessary, and the Government realized that it was necessary, that these productive enterprises should be pushed to a conclusion. It reminds me very much of a story of a man who had fallen from a high building and who was ' asked if the fall had hurt him. No, he said, the fall did not hurt me, but it was stopping so quickly. The fall is not what would hurt us in this particular ease, but it would be stopping so quickly that, would injure the credit of Canada throughout the world. So that the Minister of Finance, in putting on the brakes gradually in order to bring about a slowing up during the past year, has pursued a course which should be commended by this House.
My hon. friend also endeavoured to gain some consolation from a quotation he made from a statement by the present Prime Minister in the days when he was in Opposition, to the effect that an enormous expenditure was prima facie evidence of corruption. If my hon. friend desired to urge that there is prima facie evidence of corruption in the expenditure of the past year, or the expenditure of the year preceding that, let me say to him that



maintaining for the investment that has been made the traffie which will make it possible for the railways to earn a legitimate return.
. I have reached the end of what I desire to say, because I do not wish to deal at any considerable length with this tariff question to-night. The hon. Minister of Finance stated that we were about to enter upon a year when we would all have to be content to make certain sacrifies; that it would be a year of retrenchment. I am sure we are all willing to make those sacrifices. We are all of us desirous that certain public expenditures, more particularly those in our own locality, should be successfully carried through; but we are all broadminded enough to say that for the present economy should be exercised. We can, I think, assure the Minister of Finance that in his efforts in the coming year he will meet with full support from those who generally vote with him in this House. So, in conclusion, it seems to me we have every reason to congratulate the Minister of Finance and the country upon the Budget speech which was delivered yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the speech delivered by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance yesterday was looked forward to by the people of Canada with more interest than any Budget speech that has been delivered in this House for many years past. The reason for that is that Canada now is unfortunately experiencing a period of very great depression, a depression that is revealed in the great falling off in the revenues of the country, in the trade of the country, in the revenues of the railway companies, in the returns of the clearing houses of the banks, and in the immigration to this country. But my hon. friend the Minister of Finance told us that the depression was practically over, and that, with the opening up of ' Spring, Canada would go and prosper. There must have fallen upon my hon. friend the Minister of Finance at least a much better mantle of prophecy than he has been carrying on his shoulders for the #last six months. I remember him .saying in Montreal six months ago that there had been a depression, but that the depression at that time was all over. He was backed [DOT]by his leader the right hon. the Prime Minister who also stated that the depression was over and that Canada had entered on an era of prosperity such as she had never had in the past. When the House

opened in January, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance acknowledged that there was a depression, but stated that it would soon pass over. Therefore I think the people of Canada will be justified in taking with a very large grain of salt the statement of my hon. friend that the depression is now over.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance stated that this depression existed throughout the world. I do not know where he got that information. Be certainly did not get it from the trade returns of Great Britain, the greatest trading nation on the face of the globe. There is no depression in Great Britain. During last year and the year before there has been one of the greatest periods of prosperity ever experienced in Great Britain, which is a free trade country so that the prosperity there has not been due to protection. Therefore the depression has not existed throughout the world, and my hon. friend will have to revise his opinion if he still thinks that the depression in Canada is only a part of what exists throughout the whole world. My hon. friend for Thunder Bay and Rainy River (Mr. Carrick) did not consider that thei'e was no depression when he was speaking in the House a few weeks, ago. He pointed out that conditions were in a very grave state of depression,
10 p.m. especially as regards the iron and steel industries. The depression existing to-day is much greater than it was six months ago or even three months ago, and there has not been a time since the Conservative party went out of power in 1896 wiien there has been such a great depression existing throughout the Dominion of Canada as exists to-day. There are more men idle to-day than ever before in the history of Canada. While speaking to one of the greatest financiers in Canada a month or two ago, I mentioned that the orders from the West to the manufacturers of the East had been cut in two. ' Why,' he said, ' to my knowledge they have been cut in four or five.' I heard a manufacturer in Montreal stating within the past month that from one end of Canada to the other he questioned whether the factories were running more than half the time: I do not know whether that statement i3 correct or not, hut this gentleman is a manufacturer and he ought to know. Does that look as if the depression was over? What has caused the depression? What step3 have been taken by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to remedy the depression?

What is the basic industry of this country? Agriculture. What probably is the next greatest industry? Manufacturing-that is one of the great industries at all events. How do you benefit the farmers who form half the people of Canada-what is it that makes them prosperous? They have the land, the climate affords favourable conditions; all you need to make the farmer prosperous is a market for his product. And on whom do the manufacturers depend chiefly for their success? I leave it to the Minister of Finance himself if it is not the money that is produced out of the soil of Canada that is at the root of all prosperity in this country. If the farmers are not prosperous, how can the manufacturers be prosperous? What does the farmer do with the money he gets? He does not bury it in the ground; he spends it chiefly in manufactured goods after all. That money goes into the villages, then to the cities, and then to pay the men who have made the goods that he has consumed. But the Minister of Finance refuses to give the farmer a market and increases the very cause that has led to the depression-over-production of manufacturing. Instead of remedying matters he increases the load that the farmers have to bear.
The hon. member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) has made a few statements to which I wish to refer briefly. I notice that he, very truthfully, gives credit to the late Government for having inaugurated the Hudson Bay railway. But let me tell my hon. friend that all his colleagues from the West, and the press there supporting hon. gentlemen opposite, give all the credit to this Government for initiating that enterprise. They never say that the late Government had decided to build the road and had let t'he contract for a part of it; they take all the credit to this Government for having undertaken the construction of that railway. However, the hon. member for St. Antoine was right in that matter. He also referred to the fact that during the last year or two the Government had to pay out a considerable amount of money for railway subsidies under laws that were passed at the instance of the late Government. He forgot to tell the House that last year this Government made a gift of some sixteen and a half or fifteen and a half millions to the Canadian Northern Railway Company, and a great deal of that was paid out during last year. And, if the late Government expended too much in railway subsidies, what about this gift to Mackenzie and Mann?-for it was simply a gift. It is no
use for anybody to say: We got $7,000,000 of the common stock of the company. I say, the Government did not get $7,000,000 in the common stock of the company. The common stock that had been issued was not affected; they simply printed $7,000,000 more for this Government, and $7,000,000 to put in their own safe. But the hon. member for St. Antoine forgot to mention that. Then, if all reports are true, the gift of sixteen and a half millions to Mackenzie and Mann that would enable about $12,000,000 to go into the Canadian Northern railway and about four millions into the pockets of Bill and Dan, is to be supplemented this year by a much larger gift in the way of guarantees.

If the hon. member will
allow me: I may have inadvertently made a statement not strictly accurate in connection with the subsidy for the Canadian Northern Ontario railway. What I wanted to say was that the Canadian Northern Ontario railway subsidy of $12,800,000 paid this year largely was made necessary on account of legislation which was passed in 1911-not that it was authorized by legislation passed in 1911, but that it was made necessary by that legislation.
That is a different statement-
I did not intend to make a misstatement; I desire only that the hon. gentleman clearly understand what I meant.

Of course, the hon. gentleman would not deliberately make a mistake, but the fact remains that if he criticises the late Government for giving subsidies to the Canadian Northern railway and other railways how does he better the position of this Government by going away beyond and giving an additional sixteen and one-half millions? It was not rendered necessary by any previous legislation, in my judgment, for the simple' reason that the owners of the Canadian Northern railway could very easily have put back sixteen and one-half millions of funds that they have taken out of the unfortunate Eritish bond-holders and out of the people of this country in subsidies and guarantees from the different provinces and this Government and the previous Government. They d;d not have to come to this House; they could have put up the money out of their own pockets. But do you think they would do that? Oh, no; they have not

come to that; they are not built that way. And my hon. friend, while criticising the previous Government ' raises ' them with this fifteen and one-half or sixteen and one-half million.
The hon. gentleman took a good deal of credit for the present Government for surpluses, and gave the total of the surpluses for the fifteen or sixteen years of Liberal rule at $167,000,000, and the total of the surpluses for the three years of the present Administration at $130,000,000. But when hon. gentlemen opposite came into office they found a surplus of $38,000,000 in the treasury, and they surely cannot take credit for that. Had the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ames) been exactly fair he would have given the figures for Liberal rule not at $167,000,000 but at $205,000,000, and for the present Government not at $130,000,000, but $92,000,000. Hon. gentlemen opposite, I know, do not always consider it necessary to be exact. But my hon. friend from St. Antoine rather prides himself on being pretty handy at figures, and I should have thought that he could have come a good deal nearer to being right than he managed to do.

My authority is the public
accounts.

That is a good excuse.
But the hon. gentleman knows as well as any man in this House that that is not a fair statement-although the public accounts are all right. He knows that his friends found a surplus of $38,000,000 in the treasury when they came into power.
My hon. friend had a good deal to say about the junior member for Halifax having made reference to the fact that the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway which were purchased were at present worth only about seventy-five cents on the dollar. It was not the junior member for Halifax who made that statement; it was the Minister of Finance who made that statement yesterday and the junior member for Halifax was only quoting the words of the hon. Finance Minister in his Budget Speech. My hon. friend also gave great credit to the Finance Minister-and I am not going to say anything against that-for his good judgment in going slow in granting subsidies to railways. I only hope that my hon. friend will follow that up and that when the Finance Minister comes to deal with the tremendous demands which are now being made on this country by the Canadian Northern railway he will be able to induce the Finance Min-
ister to go slow. That is a matter that we can discuss better when it comes up in the regular way.
My hon. friend from St. Antoine division took up the question of new markets, and in that he was rather more vague than he usually is. I shall not blame him for being vague on that question. How can he help being vague on that question? We have had the Minister of Trade and Commerce travelling all over creation during the past two years trying to find new markets for Canada. He made a deal with the West Indies, a twopenny-halfpenny deal in connection with which we will spend far more in subsidizing steamers to carry what little trade can be got than the trade is worth. He spent months in Australia and New Zealand trying to make a deal but he could not do it. He went over to China and Japan and now he tells us that the Chinaman and the Jap are going to commence to eat flour and that there will be a market for Canadian wheat and flour in far-off Asia.
I think it is an acknowledged fact that the home market is the best market, and also that the nearer you get your market to home the better for the producers of the articles you have to sell. The Minister of Trade and Commerce is going to do such great things in the future, according to my hon. friend from St. Antoine; he is going to put a blue book on the table, a report that is going to change the whole face of nature and provide a market for the Canadian farmers. Unless his success in the future is a great deal better than it has been in the past two or three years it will nol amount to very much, although my hon. friend from St. Antoine says: Wait a little. But if hon. members on the Government . benches want us to get a market for the producers of Canada, is it necessary to run to Australia and New Zealand and China and Japan? There is a market right at their own door, a market awaiting them, a market in the country of the richest people on earth, people who want our goods, people who have got the money to pay for our goods. That market is there, open at rar door, open for acceptance by the people of Canada. S'et my-non. friends on the Treasury Benches, like the dog in the ' manager, will not allow the people of Canada to have that market, they will not allow the Canadian farmer to get the best out of his own product; but they say, we will send our Minister of Trade and Commerce to try and educate the Japanese and Chinamen to eat flour and then we will

be able to send a few shiploads of wheat to China and Japan. And the hon. member for St. Antoine says wait a little while, you will get your market there.
Would the hon. member consider a country a good market for Canadian produce that has more of the same kind of produce at home than they can use, for which they have to find a market abroad?

I consider a country a good market for Canadian wheat that will buy the wheat and pay the money, and I do not care if they send ten times as much out. I would ask my hon. friend where the western farmer is going to sell his wheat five years from now.
He will have to sell it to some country that needs it. I consider the United States as good a market for our wheat as Wales is for our coal.

My hon. friend says that you have to sell your wheat in some country that needs it. How many countries are we selling to now? One country, and that country never takes more than one-fifth of what she wants from Canada, and what is more, it is doubtful if she ever will. Why? Because there is a crop of wheat ripening in every month of the year in some quarter of the gloUe. She sends her ships with British goods to those countries. Do you think she is going to bring those ships home empty and then send them over to Canada for Canadian wheat when she can buy it there, and buy it cheaper in many cases? Not at all. You have got to get another - market for the western farmer in wheat or only one thing can follow, and that is that the western farmer has got to go out of growing wheat. You cannot dump all the wheat that we will have to export in a few years on England, even if England took her whole wheat supply from Canada. But, as I said, she will never take more than one-fifth to one-quarter of her wheat from Canada. My hon. friend asks: How can you sell wheat to the United States when they export wheat themselves? We can sell wheat to the United States when they want to buy it, and conditions are becoming such in the United States that there is a great deal of land now growing wheat that is growing wheat at a loss, and that they will have to take out of wheat growing. You must have one of two conditions to produce wheat, either cheap land or cheap labour. In the United States they have neither cheap land nor cheap
labour, and on land that is worth $100 an acre there is not a man on earth can grow wheat and get interest on his money at the present prices of wheat.

Notwithstanding that,
they have 80,000,000 bushels of wheat annually to export.
My hon friend is astray if he says they export 80,000,000 bushels of wheat.
I have the United States statistics from the Agricultural Department at Washington direct.

At all events, the American people offer to buy our wheat, they offer to pay higher prices for it than we can get at home, and is that not enough for our farmers ? Why do our farmers need to go beyond that ? Why does each individual farmer need to bother his head whether the United States buy that wheat from him and then export a bushel of their soft wheat. The reason the American people want our wheat is because it is a hard wheat. Only a small portion of the United States can grow wheat of the quality we raise in Manitoba. The state of North Dakota and part of Minnesota grow the hard wheat, but all the other states produce the soft wheat, which does not make the class of flour that the people of the United States want. They have to mix one bushel of hard wheat with every four bushels of soft wheat in order to get the desired quality of flour. That is why the Canadian farmer can get more for his wheat in the United States than anywhere else, and that is why the farmer in North Dakota gets more for his wheat than the farmer 500 miles south of him. That i3 quite plain. But yet hon. gentlemen opposite, including members on the Government benches, have argued time and again that wheat is not dearer in the United States than in Canada, and they very dishonestly quote No. 1 and 2 Manitoba Northern as against No. 1 and No. 2 Minneapolis. My hon. friend the Minister of Public Works knows perfectly well that No. 1 Manitoba Northern is a different wheat altogether from No. 1 Minneapolis Northern. He knows that No. 2 Manitoba Northern is much better wheat than No. 1 Minneapolis Northern, and that No. 3 Manitoba Northern is in many cases a great deal better than No. 1 Minneapolis Northern.
Does not my hon. friend know that they have no fixed grade for wheat in the United States ?

My hon. friend shows how little he knows about the subject. I propose to give my hon. friend some information on the subject of grades in Minneapolis. He says they have no stated grade. Here is what the Act says:
No. 1 Northern spring wheat shall be dry, sound, sweet and clean, may consist of the hard and soft varieties of spring wheat and weigh not less than 57 pounds to the measured bushel.
No. 2 Northern spring wheat shall be dry, spring wheat, not clean enough or sound enough for No. 1, but of good milling quality and must not weigh less than 56 pounds to the measured bushel.
No. 3 Northern spring wheat shall be composed of inferior, shrunken spring wheat and weigh not less than 54 pounds to the measured bushel.
What I stated was that there was no general grade for wheat in the United States. Every state has its own grade, and in .several places the wheat is graded by the different hoards of trade.

Let us contrast No. 1 Manitoba Northern against the Minneapolis grades:
No. 1 Manitoba Northern wheat shall be sound and well cleaned, weighing not less than 60 pounds to the bushel, and shall be composed of at least 60 per cent of hard red Fife wheat.
No. 2 Manitoba Northern wheat shall be soound and reasonably clean, of good milling qualities and fit for warehousing, weighing not less than 58 pounds to the bushel, and shall be composed of at least 45 per cent of hard red Fife wheat.
Any wheat not good enough to be graded as No. 2 Manitoba Northern shall be graded No. 3 Manitoba Northern in the discretion of the inspector.
So that if there was only 40 per cent of hard Red Fife wheat it would not be classed as No. 2 Manitoba Northern, but would be graded No. 3, and we would have *a wheat weighing 58 lbs. to the bushel graded as No. 3 Manitoba Northern that had 40 per cent Red Fife wheat in it; whereas No. 1 Minneapolis Northern only has to weigh the same, and does not need to have one grain of Red Fife wheat in it; It will also be seen that there is a difference of 3 lbs. to the bushel between No. 1 Manitoba Northern and No. 1 Minneapolis Northern, and that No. 1 Manitoba Northern has to have at least 60 per cent of hard Red Fife wheat, whereas No. 1 Minnesota does not need to have any hard Red Fife wheat at all. Any one can see how absolutely unfair it is to quote No. 1 Manitoba Northern against No. 1 Minneapolis Northern, but that is just exactly what 
hon. gentlemen opposite and the Conservative press throughout the country are doing and have been doing right along. I have heard the Minister of Finance himself doing the same thing, but I do not think he will do it again, as he knows better now.
As I .said before, only two states on the other side of the line can grow anything like the quality of wheat we grow in the West, so you can understand, Mr. Speaker, why hard wheat grown in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan commands a much higher price in the United States than the softer wheat that is grown in most of their states. It has been the custom of * hon. gentlemen opposite and their press to take the quotations for the month of July or August. For a week or so in those months wheat is quoted at a lower price in Winnipeg than in Minneapolis, but even then, considering that No. 3 Manitoba Northern is about equal to No. 1 Minneapolis Northern, the Winnipeg price is (really better. Hon. gentlemen opposite quote the figures just at that time of the year to show that Canada has lost nothing by not having free trade in wheat. There are times in the months of July and August, when no wheat practically is coming into the Winnipeg market, and when any wheat that has been carried over the winter has been marketed, that shippers who have engaged space in the steamers carrying wheat across the lakes and the ocean find that they are short of wheat and they have to get an extra 10,000, or 20,000, or 50,000 bushels to make good their contracts and occupy their space and then perhaps for a week or two wheat may jump two or three cents. The farmers are not bringing in any wheat and it is just a matter of speculation. The farmers of the West are losing millions of dollars a year on account of the refusal of this Government to take advantage of the offer that was made under the tariff of the United States in October last. Millions and millions of dollar are being lost by the farmaris, and at whose instigation ?-the millers and the railways. The Minister of Public Works knows that free wheat would be to the advantage of the farmer. When my hon. friend was in the province of Manitoba not many months ago, participating in the Macdonald election, he made a very ingenious promise to the farmers he was talking to there as a result of which every one of them believed that he had promised them free wheat. Other speakers went

through the country promising them free wheat. One of his particular friends introduced a resolution into the Manitoba Legislature recommending free wheat. Yet we find that hon. members opposite representing Manitoba constituencies all voted against free wheat. Do they think that all the local members are wrong? Do they think that they have made a mistake? Does my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works believe that free wheat would not be to the advantage of the farmers of Manitoba and that the members of the Manitoba Legislature were wrong?
Was there a vote in the legislature?

There was a vote in the legislature and every member of the legislature, Conservative and Liberal alike, recommended this Government to accept the offer of the Government of the United States and put wheat on the free list. The hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaffner) who, I am sorry is not in his seat just now, stated not long ago in the House that he represented eighty-five per cent of the voters in his constituency and that he brought their thanks to the Government for what they had done for the western farmers. I would like to ask my hon. friend if he thinks that in voting against free wheat he represented eighty-five per cent- of his constituents? My hon. friend in 1908 had a majority of 650 and in 1911, because he was against reciprocity, his majority was cut down to 62.
But the argument that was put up then that we were giving a great deal for reciprocity cannot be put up against free wheat. The American people have offered us free wheat and hon. members from the province of Manitoba will have something to explain to their people when they go back. I would venture the statement, Mr. Speaker, that no hon. member of this House can go to the farmers of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, or Alberta and get any farmers' organization to pass a resolution endorsing the action of the Government in refusing free (wheat. . You can feet individual farmers; that is easily done. That can be accomplished, that can toe staged, that can be organized exactly as the delegation that was brought down here to oppose free wheat was organized, but you cannot get any one farmers' organization in the West, and I doubt very much if you can get a farmers' organization in the East, to endorse the action of the Government, in refusing free wheat.
The Minister of Finance said that you have to protect the farmer. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, if he were here, who are the best judges as to whether they want protection or not? I would like to ask the Minister of Finance, and in his absence, I will ask the hon. Minister of Public Works, who is leading the House, if any industry in Canada would have protection imposed upon it if it did not desire it. Take the woollen industry or the cotton industry; supposing a delegation elected to represent these industries came to this Government and said: We have had protection a good while, we are in such shape now that if protection were wiped out and our product put on the free list it would enable us to hold our own market at home and increase our exports very materially, to make more money and do more business-would not my hon. friend think that he would toe absolutely justified in saying that these manufacturers of woollen and cotton goods were the people who ought to know best and that if they did not want protection, protection should not be forced down their throats? Yet that is exactly what the Government are doing with the farmer. The farmer says that he does not want protection. The farmer says that protection on wheat is no good to him, that it does not give him anything but the Government say: You do not know what you are talking about; protection is good for you, and you must have it whether you like it or not.
I would like to read an article by a farmer dealing with this very question, and I may say that I happen to know this farmer very well. He lives in my constituency. I have been through some seven or eight elections and this gentleman was one of the most able, sturdy and dangerous opponents that I had for many years, and one who did more against me in several of my elections than any other man in that part of the country. He had the ability. He was a Conservative of the Conservatives, an Orangeman among the Orangemen, a real, genuine Orange Conservative in the old days and a good one. He is_ a high-class man, but he was so bitter in his politics that he could not see anything but: vote Conservative. That man happens to be living close to the boundary line, and he has for a good many years sold a great deal of his farm products in the United States. He is the manager of, or helps to manage, an elevator at the town of Sherwood, in Dakota, owned almost altogether by Canadian farmers living in this vicinity. I would like to give you his views on the wheat question. These are the views of an actual farmer, a man

who grows thousands of bushels of grain every year himself, and who raises a good deal of stock. These remarks were made at a meeting of the municipal officers held in the city of Regina about a month ago. This article is published in the Regina Leader of March 5:
Free wheat must come to farmers' aid-Municipality of Argyle is striking example of need of American market-Paying duty to States-Farmers do better in United States market even when handicapped by tariff.
J. G. Burke, reeve of the municipality of Argyle, and a delegate at the Rural Municipalities' Convention in session at the city hall, is a strong advocate of reciprocity. Mr. Burke at one time was a Conservative but is now devoting both time and energy in the interests of reciprocity as the one solution to the marketing of western grain.
' Why should I not support reciprocity,' asked Mr. Burke.
' When you consider that in the southern part of the municipality of Argyle, including Mount Pleasant, in the past several years the sum of $50,000 has been lost to the farmers by reason of the duty on grain, the injustice of the present duty is at once 'apparent. If all the grain in that district had been shipped to the States the amount would have been three times as great.'
' While the construction of the proposed Georgian Bay canal and the deepening of the St. Lawrence river and Great Lakes waterways would no doubt be a great help in the marketing of the western grain,' said Mr. Burke, ' the quickest, the best and the only solution is reciprocity. Millions have already been spent in the deepening of these waterways, and the result has been that the freight rates have increased. We have no assurance that the freight rates would be reduced with the completion of these proposed works. What we want is reciprocity.'
Ninety per cent of the grain grown in southern Argyle was already being shipped to the States, Mr. Burke pointed out. Forty per cent of the grain produced in the whole municipality from the fall of 1912 to November 21, 1913, 350,000 bushels of grain from southern Argyle, had been shipped through the two outlets, Antler and Sherwood, North Dakota. Duty was paid on one-third of that amount, or a little more than 100,000 bushels. The rest went through in bond. If the American market remained high enough all the time, the farmers of the district would prefer to ship all their grain by way of the south and pay the duty.
Continuing, Mr. Burke said: ' The duty on wheat is 10 cents, on barley 15, and on flax 20 cents. In November last, for flax grown on my own farm and shipped south, I paid a duty amounting to $187. From the middle of September up until a week ago, the average American flax has been from 20 to 21 cents per bushel higher than Canadian flax of similar grades. In November, I received from $1.01 to $1.09 per bushel for all the flax I sold in the States. I realized anywhere from one to ten cents more per bushel by shipping my flax to the States, even after the duty was paid. Why should I not be in favour of reciprocity and with the doing away of the duty? '
Mr. Burke quoted the instance of a man who
IMr. Turriff.]
had a car of potatoes for sale last fall. From inquiries at Winnipeg in October, he found that the best he could get was thirty-five cents per bushel for his potatoes, bagged and all, while in Iowa he could get $1 per bushel. After paying 22 cents per bushel for freight and six cents for duty he realized 73 or 74 cents per bushel by selling them in the States. Mr. Burke believed the States would always be in a position to draw heavily on the resources of Canada, especially in wheat products, because of the inferior quality of wheat grown in the States. They would always require a large quantity of good hard wheat, while in Canada there was no market for barley at all.
These are the views of a farmer who knows what he is talking about; a man who grows the grain and pays the duty and sells his product in the United States, and gets a considerably higher price for it than he would in Canada. And, when the proposition was made by the United States to put wheat on the free list, this Canadian Government turned it down. At whose instigation? At the instigation of the millers and of the railways. For every dollar that the millers have invested in Canada, the farmers of Canada have one thousand invested; for every dollar the Canadian millers pay out in wages, the Canadian farmers pay out one thousand dollars. The farmers of Canada have more money invested than have the railways, while in the case of the farmers it is their own money, and in the case of the railways one-half of it is practically the money of the farmers. But still this Government listens to the railways, and they have turned the farmers down cold, absolutely cold. What did the farmers get out of the Budget of yesterday?

Five per cent on
agricultural implements.

No Sir, they did not,
*and the statement of my hon. friend shows just how much he knows about it. The hon. gentleman cannot be a farmer; he is probably a gentleman who farms the farmer. What the farmer got was a reduction of five per cent on binders and mowers, but the tariff on the other implements is kept up. My hon. friend from North Ontario (Mr. Sharpe) a.s usual is flip, and he is wrong. The proposition under the reciprocity agreement was a reduction of two and a half per cent on these items, and five per cent off everything else, and yet my hon. friend says that five per cent on two items is more than the Liberals offered to the farmers. Who stopped them

from getting the benefits of the reciprocity treaty? Hon. gentlemen opposite did.

My hon. friend has made a mistake, and I am sure he does not wish to misstate the case. He used the words: ' five pei cent on everything else.' In the reciprocity pact there was no reduction provided for in the case of threshers.

If I made a mistake I am very glad to be corrected, but I can very soon state what the five per cent was proposed to be given on. It was on, hay-rakes, manure-spreaders, drills, seeders of all kinds, disc-harrows, double-discs, shoe-drills, grass-seed attachment for drills, cultivators, ploughs, scuffiers, and wagons. I notice that the Minister of Finance did not announce any reduction in the duty on ploughs. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) evidently was able to step in and prevent that. The hon. gentleman could sell a Cockshutt plough in the United States, years ago, and pay a fifteen per cent duty, and 45 per cent duty on the repairs, and undersell, or compete to the extent of selling trainloads in the United States. But the 'Cockshutt Plough 'Company does not want any reduction of the duty in Canada. The hon. gentleman would not even be satisfied with the five per cent reduction, bringing the tariff down from twenty to fifteen per cent; he must have the full pound of flesh. There are farmers in my constituency who came from the United States and who brought over Cockshutt steam-gang or gasoline gang-ploughs which they bought in the United States, after a duty of fifteen per cent had been paid on them. These ploughs have gone as faT west from the factory as 400 miles west from Winnipeg, and these settlers bought them in the United States and brought them into Canada, and when they went to the Cockshutt office in Weyburn to get another plough of the 'same sort, they found they had to pay from $100 to $110 more for that same plough that they brought into Canada without paying duty. There is no reduction to the farmer on anything but binders and mowers, and when they reduced protection' by five per cent on these items, the Government immediately put on far more in the duties on iron and steel. A farmer will buy a binder every eight or ten years, and the Government take off five per cent, which means a reduction of about $5 in the duty. But every time he buys a keg or a pound of nails, a paper of tacks or anything made of iron or steel,
something which he do^-s every day in the year, under the tariff ns announced yesterday, for the reduction of $5 on his binder and $2.50 on his mower, or a total of $7.50, he will pay $35 or $40 in the increased cost of the articles on which the duty was put yesterday by placing iron and steel in the dutiable list. It was a cold deal handed out to the farmers yesterday, the coldest deal ever handed out to them.
Mr. WM. SMITH: Poor farmers!
Yes, poor farmers.
We can stand it.

Yes, you can stand it, no doubt. Political farmers can, but the farmers who have sent you here may have-something to say about the matter. A good deal of explanation will be required,, and my genial friend the Minister of Publie Works will have something to do to get away from the promises the farmers thought he made. I acknowledge that my hon. friend has left a loophole to escape through. Oh, yes, and he will crawl through it all right; but this refusal to give free wheat will cost the party a good many votes, and this cold deal of taking off $5 and adding on $20 to material made of iron and steel bought by the farmers, will require a great deal of explanation in the West. I do not believe even my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Ames), with. his magic lantern, will be able to explain that away in the West.
